rationale: A wins because it turns the same thin announcement into three reportable lanes: operations, missing resale economics, and ownership-structure constraints. Its best line, "Half a million secondhand Patagonia items later, the company still won't say if resale pays," names the tension instead of polishing the stat. B has decent bones, but "A sustainable-fashion or circular-economy trade reporter" and "right to repair" drift toward generic beat wallpaper, and the third angle partly duplicates the second instead of earning its own slot.
gaps_in_A: "category-creation" is a little grand for an all-store/mail-in expansion of an existing program; the actual story is retail operations, not a new category being born.

"A company with no shareholders is giving away repairs — nobody else can copy the math" overstates what the update proves. Patagonia's structure is relevant, but "nobody else can copy" needs cost data and competitor evidence.
The first angle says other retailers "will be asked about" this. Plausible, but not in the fact set; it should be framed as a reporting question, not a given.
gaps_in_B: "right to repair" is an outside peg the update did not provide. It may be relevant, but here it is imported decoration until sourced.
The second and third angles both orbit the same missing denominator: "will not say what share of revenue resale represents." B gets two angles from one tension and calls it distinctness.
"Patagonia says its used-gear platform has now resold over 500,000 items" is too close to the press-release fact. The stronger story is the missing context, which A leads with.
"comparable branded-resale figures the user would have to source themselves" is useful, but it punts too much of the proof burden instead of defining the exact comparison needed.
